candidates.name: State the Number First
candidates.mechanism: Whoever states the first number in a price conversation sets the frame the rest of the conversation gets measured against. Hesitating to give a number, or waiting for the customer to name a budget first, hands them control of that anchor instead of you.
candidates.evidence: Peer-reviewed research (Galinsky & Mussweiler, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) found that whichever party made the first offer in a negotiation consistently achieved a better final outcome, and that first offers were a strong predictor of the final settlement price — an advantage that held in both face-to-face and email negotiations, and only disappeared when the other party specifically focused on countering the reasoning behind that first number.
candidates.transferTemplate: When a customer asks 'how much is this going to cost?', give a real number (or a confident range) rather than deflecting with 'it depends' or waiting to see what they were hoping to pay. The number you say first becomes the anchor the rest of the conversation is measured against — hesitating just hands that anchor to whatever figure the customer already had in their head, which is often lower than what the job is actually worth.

candidates.name: Price the Outcome You Deliver, Not the Hours It Takes
candidates.mechanism: Pricing by time worked ties your income to how long a job takes, which actively punishes you for getting faster and more experienced at it, and makes every estimate a guess about hours instead of a statement about what the result is worth. Pricing around the outcome the customer actually gets removes that mismatch and gives you a real, defensible basis for the number.
candidates.evidence: Consultant Martin Krumbein, founder of the German consultancy OnTarget, switched from a traditional day-rate model to value-based pricing and reported doubling his turnover and income within a year, closing new retainer contracts priced around the documented value he created for clients (including a manufacturing client's cost savings) rather than hours logged.
candidates.transferTemplate: Instead of estimating a job purely off hours-times-rate, price around the specific outcome the customer is paying for — a working system, a passed inspection, a problem that's actually gone — and let your own experience and efficiency work in your favor instead of against you. A faster, more experienced tech currently makes less per job under hourly pricing for being good at the work; outcome-based pricing fixes that.
candidates.verificationCaveats: This is a real named person with real first-person quotes, but it's a promotional client-success story published by Consulting Success, the coaching company that helped him make the transition — not an independent study. Same credibility tier as the Quick Sprout entry approved in the Day 3 review.

candidates.name: Build a Model, Not a Gut Check
candidates.mechanism: Pricing decisions made case-by-case, by feel, are inconsistent in ways nobody can see until they're aggregated across many jobs — some underpriced, some overpriced, with no way to tell which from any single quote. Breaking pricing into a defined, repeatable model built from real data removes the guesswork from each individual estimate.
candidates.evidence: American Airlines built a formal revenue (yield) management system that broke pricing into defined sub-problems — overbooking, discount allocation, and traffic management — solved systematically rather than case-by-case. Per a peer-reviewed account in the operations research journal Interfaces, the airline estimated the quantifiable benefit at $1.4 billion over three years, with an expected ongoing annual contribution of more than $500 million.
candidates.transferTemplate: Instead of estimating each job from scratch by feel, build a simple, consistent model: a base rate for materials and labor, defined multipliers for complexity or urgency, and a documented minimum margin — then apply it the same way every time. It won't be perfect on any single job, but it removes the inconsistency (and the anxiety) of pricing every estimate as its own individual guess.
